newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF calls for fast privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF calls for fast privatisation.

text.p: French defence firm Thomson-CSF, which the government has decided to sell privately after a bungled privatisation attempt last year, called on Wednesday for its sale to go ahead as fast as possible .

"The management of Thomson-CSF takes note of this decision and is pleased that it answers some essential concerns of Thomson-CSF," a company spokesman said after the government announced the sale plan on Wednesday..

"We hope the timetable for the sale will be as short as possible because the world is moving around us," he said, referring to defence sector restructuring already taking place in the United States and Europe.
Thomson-CSF, fearing it might be swallowed up in a larger grouping by the privatisation, had lobbied for a public flotation.
But this attitude changed after the government announced it would sell Thomson-CSF by private placement and issued terms and conditions.
Thomson-CSF said it welcomed the plan for it to become a world-scale defence electronics company, while keeping a "golden share" in state hands.
The government said in a statement it was seeking to bring together many industrial capabilities around Thomson-CSF as part of the restructuring of the European defence industry.
The decision to keep a golden share would allow it to "protect national defence interests and avoid any dismantling of the company", the statement said.
The government is relaunching the privatisation of Thomson-CSF, which is 58 percent held by state-owned Thomson SA group, after cancelling its previous plan to sell the entire group in December.
The government had previously expressed a preference for a bid by Lagardere for the Thomson group over a rival bid by Alcatel Alsthom.
Alcatel has since acted to reinforce its position since last year by lining up a joint bid with state-owned aircraft and defence firm Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation for Thomson-CSF.
The Thomson-CSF spokesman said the company was pleased that employees would have access to its shares under terms similar to those available if it had been privatised through a public share offer.
Ten percent of shares sold are to be reserved for employees of Thomson and its subsidiaries.
Thomson-CSF also applauded a government commitment to associate the company closely with all stages of the sale.

Thomson-CSF shares climbed on the government announcement, trading by late morning up 4.56 percent at 183.5 francs ($32.10), the highest level this year, even though the blue-chip CAC-40 index was down 0.05 percent.
Traders said the government's decision to sell the company by private placement should lead to a better share valuation.

"The privatisation will go ahead through a private placement, quickly, and, no doubt, at a better price than through a public offering, a fund manager said. "A public offering would have scattered the capital, whereas here, they are selling control of the company and that has a cost."

Traders also said Thomson shares were benefiting simply from the fact there had been an announcement. "The government has finally given its opinion and traders are reassessing the project," a trader said.
